detail.findings_tradeoffs: Cook and Mertz (STOC 2024) give an algorithm for TreeEval running in super-logarithmic space $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and super-polynomial time $n^{O(\log\log n)}$. On the other hand, an earlier algorithm of J. Cook and Mertz (STOC 2020), run on a catalytic tape, solves TreeEval in logarithmic $O(\log n)$ free space and polynomial time, but with polynomial $O(\sqrt{n})$ catalytic space. We show that the latter result can be improved. We give a catalytic algorithm for TreeEval with logarithmic $O(\log n)$ free space, polynomial runtime, and subpolynomial $2^{O(\log^\epsilon n)}$ catalytic space (for any $\epsilon > 0$). Our result also implies an improved simulation of time by \textit{catalytic} space, via the reduction of Williams (STOC 2025). Our TreeEval algorithm comes from a framework, inspired by private information retrieval, that generically reduces tree evaluation to two combinatorial objects: matching-vector families and \emph{decoders} (a new object we define that closely resembles decoding polynomials). These ingredients' parameters directly govern an algorithm's resources: the vectors' dimension determines its catalytic space, and the decoder's sparsity determines its free space and runtime. In addition to enabling our new algorithm, this framework explains existing tradeoffs, for example why the Cook–Mertz algorithm needs super-logarithmic space but no catalytic tape. It also lets better matching-vector families or decoders plug in directly to give better algorithms.

items.headline: Dynark: Making Groth16 Dynamic
items.summary: In recent years, numerous new and more efficient constructions of zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (zkSNARK) have been proposed, motivated by their growing practical applications. However, in most schemes, when the witness is changed, the prover has to recompute the proof from scratch even if the new witness is close to the old one. This is inefficient for applications where proofs are generated for dynamically changing witnesses with small changes.

detail.problem_context: In recent years, numerous new and more efficient constructions of zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge (zkSNARK) have been proposed, motivated by their growing practical applications.
detail.method_architecture: However, in most schemes, when the witness is changed, the prover has to recompute the proof from scratch even if the new witness is close to the old one. This is inefficient for applications where proofs are generated for dynamically changing witnesses with small changes.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: In this paper, we introduce DYNARK, a dynamic zkSNARK scheme that can update the proof in sublinear time when the change of the witness is small. DYNARK is built on top of the seminal zkSNARK protocol of Groth, 2016. In the semi-dynamic setting, for an R1CS of size $n$, after a preprocessing of $O(n\log n)$ group operations on the original witness, it only takes $O(d)$ group operations and $O(d\log^2 d)$ field operations to update the proof for a new witness with distance $d$ from the original witness, which is nearly optimal. In the fully-dynamic setting, the update time of DYNARK is $O(d\sqrt{n\log n})$ group operations and $O(d\log^2 d)$ field operations. Both the proof size and the verifier time are $O(1)$, which are exactly the same as Groth16. Compared to the scheme in a prior work by Wang et al. 2024, we reduce the proof size from $O(\sqrt{n})$ to $O(1)$ without relying on pairing product arguments or another zkSNARK, and the update time and the verifier time of DYNARK are faster in practice. Experimental results show that for $n=2^{20}$, after a one-time preprocessing of 74.3 seconds, it merely takes 3 milliseconds to update the proof in our semi-dynamic zkSNARK for $d=1$, and 60 milliseconds to update the proof in our fully-dynamic zkSNARK. These are 1433$\times$ and 73$\times$ faster than Groth16, respectively. The proof size is 192 bytes and the verifier time is 4.4 milliseconds. The system is fully compatible with any existing deployment of Groth16 without changing the trusted setup, the proof and the verification algorithm.

items.headline: Linear Cryptanalysis with Bibrace Characters: Weak-Key Distinguishers for CRAFT
items.summary: Linear cryptanalysis measures the correlation of a cipher with the characters of the group used to define differences. If that group is replaced by a second elementary abelian group structure on the same set, here the one coming from a binary bibrace, then the admissible masks are no longer the ordinary scalar products: exactly half of them survive, and the other half are forced to be quadratic. Beyne's geometric approach develops linear cryptanalysis over an arbitrary finite abelian group, providing a natural framework for this setting.

detail.problem_context: Linear cryptanalysis measures the correlation of a cipher with the characters of the group used to define differences.
detail.method_architecture: If that group is replaced by a second elementary abelian group structure on the same set, here the one coming from a binary bibrace, then the admissible masks are no longer the ordinary scalar products: exactly half of them survive, and the other half are forced to be quadratic. detail.findings_tradeoffs: We instantiate it on the group of a particular bibrace and apply it to CRAFT. Over this group the MIDORI/CRAFT S-box has four probability-one relations, forming a small subgroup of the dual which the S-box preserves in both directions. A trail that stays inside that subgroup is determined by its first mask and propagates linearly, so the search for the best such trail is a minimum weight codeword problem, which we solve exactly by complete enumeration. A trail costs correlation, and it restricts the key to a weak-key class. We show that the exact reading, obtained by analysing the diffusion layer and the key addition together rather than separately, gives a class several bits larger than the one obtained cell by cell. One concrete consequence is that CRAFT's round constants, whatever their values, impose no restriction at all. On CRAFT we obtain weak-key distinguishers up to eighteen rounds. At fourteen rounds a single trail has squared correlation $2^{-44}$ over a class of $2^{108}$ keys, against $2^{-62.12}$ for the designers' linear hull, which is the best known linear result on the cipher and holds for all keys. On that class the trail alone therefore exceeds the best linear correlation by eighteen bits at equal round count. Half of the optimal trails begin and end with ordinary linear masks, so these are linear approximations of CRAFT in the usual sense. A contrasting analysis of MIDORI64, which shares the S-box, traces its protection to the round constants and describes two known invariants of that cipher through other bibraces.

Over this group the MIDORI/CRAFT S-box has four probability-one relations, forming a small subgroup of the dual which the S-box preserves in both directions. A trail that stays inside that subgroup is determined by its first mask and propagates linearly, so the search for the best such trail is a minimum weight codeword problem, which we solve exactly by complete enumeration. A trail costs correlation, and it restricts the key to a weak-key class. We show that the exact reading, obtained by analysing the diffusion layer and the key addition together rather than separately, gives a class several bits larger than the one obtained cell by cell. One concrete consequence is that CRAFT's round constants, whatever their values, impose no restriction at all. On CRAFT we obtain weak-key distinguishers up to eighteen rounds. At fourteen rounds a single trail has squared correlation $2^{-44}$ over a class of $2^{108}$ keys, against $2^{-62.12}$ for the designers' linear hull, which is the best known linear result on the cipher and holds for all keys. On that class the trail alone therefore exceeds the best linear correlation by eighteen bits at equal round count. Half of the optimal trails begin and end with ordinary linear masks, so these are linear approximations of CRAFT in the usual sense. A contrasting analysis of MIDORI64, which shares the S-box, traces its protection to the round constants and describes two known invariants of that cipher through other bibraces.

items.headline: Can Home Visits Re-Engage Chronically Absent Students? Evidence from the LEAP Program -- by Eric Brunner, Shangyue Jiang, Stephen Ross
items.summary: Beginning in the summer of 2021, the state of Connecticut launched the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program (LEAP) where home visits by school personnel were conducted with students identified as chronically absent from Connecticut’s 15 most disadvantaged school districts. Home visits were designed to connect students and their families directly with teachers to foster strong connections. We use student-level data from 2021–22 through 2023-24 to estimate event studies of the effect of LEAP on student attendance, chronic absenteeism, disciplinary incidents, and student achievement.

items.headline: Unraveling the Cobweb of Global Imbalances: Drivers, Vulnerabilities and Adjustment Scenarios -- by Stefan Avdjiev, Kristin Forbes, Tsvetelina Nenova, Marjorie Santos
items.summary: This paper analyses the evolution and drivers of the stock of global imbalances in order to assess associated vulnerabilities and potential adjustment scenarios. These imbalances have recently increased sharply, with a deterioration in the US net international investment position (NIIP) mirrored by NIIP improvements in most other major economies. We decompose these NIIP changes into their proximate drivers for a sample of 28 economies and find that financial factors (including valuation changes and investment income flows) are the primary drivers of global imbalances at both short and long horizons, while trade also plays a significant role (especially at long horizons).

items.headline: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
items.summary: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S.

items.headline: Ab initio simulation of excited-state potential energy surfaces with transferable deep quantum Monte Carlo
items.summary: Nature Computational Science, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43588-026-01065-y Transferable deep-learning quantum Monte Carlo for molecular excited states is introduced. Sharing parameters, an ansatz represents the wavefunction across molecular geometries and states, reducing the cost of modeling potential energy surfaces.
items.headline_tr: Aktarılabilir derin kuantum Monte Carlo ile uyarılmış durum potansiyel enerji yüzeylerinin Ab initio simülasyonu
items.summary_tr: Nature Computational Science, Çevrimiçi yayınlandı: 06 Kasım 2026; doi:10.1038/s43588-026-01065-y Moleküler uyarılmış durumlar için aktarılabilir derin öğrenme kuantumu Monte Carlo tanıtıldı. Parametreleri paylaşan bir ansatz, moleküler geometriler ve durumlar arasındaki dalga fonksiyonunu temsil ederek potansiyel enerji yüzeylerini modelleme maliyetini azaltır.

items.headline: Information Elicitation by Ordinal Agreement
items.summary: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models. In many such settings, there is no objective ground truth against which reports can be directly verified, making incentive-compatible elicitation challenging. Peer-prediction mechanisms have been designed to achieve truthful elicitation despite the lack of ground-truth verification.

detail.problem_context: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models.
detail.method_architecture: In many such settings, there is no objective ground truth against which reports can be directly verified, making incentive-compatible elicitation challenging. Peer-prediction mechanisms have been designed to achieve truthful elicitation despite the lack of ground-truth verification.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: However, existing peer-prediction methods do not provide incentives for agents to truthfully compress rich private information (e.g. reviews) into coarser ordinal reports (e.g. rankings) requested by the mechanisms. We propose a simple ordinal peer-prediction mechanism that rewards agents based on pairwise agreement, measured by Kendall tau. Under a broad class of Bayesian Stochastically Order Consistent models---which includes classical models such as Mallows and Thurstone---we prove that truthful reporting is stochastically dominant, and strongly truthful under index-equivariant strategies. This provides robust incentives even for agents with non-linear utility functions, such as risk aversion. Our mechanism further accommodates heterogeneous agents, top-K reports, and subset assignments, where each agent is scored against one randomly drawn peer. Experiments on synthetic Mallows and Thurstone data, together with a real-data stress test on the SUSHI preference dataset, show right-shifted truthful-payment distributions and the highest normalized sensitivity among tested baselines.

items.headline: A Sequential Framework for Urban Drone Delivery: Network Design, Vehicle Sizing, and Energy and Cost Assessment
items.summary: A sequential engineering framework is presented for urban drone delivery, linking hub location, route planning, mission-specific vehicle sizing, and energy and operating cost assessment. Aggregate origin-destination demand is assumed known a priori. For each hub configuration, the maximum required link distance is minimized, and feasible routes that return to their departure hubs are generated.

detail.problem_context: A sequential engineering framework is presented for urban drone delivery, linking hub location, route planning, mission-specific vehicle sizing, and energy and operating cost assessment.
detail.method_architecture: Aggregate origin-destination demand is assumed known a priori. For each hub configuration, the maximum required link distance is minimized, and feasible routes that return to their departure hubs are generated.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Route frequencies are determined using mixed-integer linear programming to satisfy delivery demand. The resulting range requirement guides motor-propeller selection and battery sizing to minimize vehicle takeoff mass. Flight distances and frequencies, cruise performance, and vehicle dimensions are combined to estimate monthly energy consumption, fleet size, hub area, staffing, and operating cost. The framework is applied to district-level Seoul delivery data. Increasing the number of hubs from one to four reduces the required range from 30.6 to 21.9 km and vehicle takeoff mass from 8.12 to 6.12 kg. Despite a 21.5% increase in total flight distance, monthly flight energy consumption decreases by 13.1%, from 15.2 to 13.2 MWh. Battery replacement is the largest vehicle-related operating expense, while operating cost per delivery increases from USD 1.18 to USD 2.20 because of higher rent and labor costs at the hubs. Among the designs evaluated, range-matched vehicles achieve the lowest operating cost in the two- and four-hub networks; a longer-range vehicle is least costly in the three-hub network. Sensitivity analyses further examine the effects of delivery demand and operating assumptions. The results demonstrate that reductions in vehicle mass and energy consumption do not necessarily lead to lower system operating cost.

items.headline: Solvable macroscopic models for populations of type I excitability neurons with Gaussian noise
items.summary: The dynamics of type I excitability neurons near the bifurcation point are governed by the model of quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron (QIF). The model of QIF subject to white Gaussian noise is abundant in statistical physics, since it not only reasonably reproduces the dynamics of some biological systems but also emerges in the problems of stochastic stability and in quantum mechanics of one-dimensional systems with quenched disorder. We derive the solution for the mean interspike interval of a QIF subject to additive Gaussian noise in terms of analytic functions, from the first passage time problem.

Beyaz Gauss gürültüsüne maruz kalan QIF modeli, istatistiksel fizikte bol miktarda bulunur, çünkü yalnızca bazı biyolojik sistemlerin dinamiklerini makul bir şekilde yeniden üretmekle kalmaz, aynı zamanda stokastik kararlılık problemlerinde de ortaya çıkar.

items.headline: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
items.summary: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures.

items.headline: Vibration patterns and reed - pipe coupling in the free reeds of the hulusi
items.summary: The hulusi is a free-reed instrument from Yunnan, Western China, known for its unique sound. Its reed and frame are cut from a single brass sheet in a symmetric shape, the free end narrower than the clamped end. Its free reeds are coupled to tubes that determine the instrument's pitch during normal playing.

detail.method_architecture: Its reed and frame are cut from a single brass sheet in a symmetric shape, the free end narrower than the clamped end. Its free reeds are coupled to tubes that determine the instrument's pitch during normal playing.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: With reduced playing pressure, the reed frequency takes over the instrument sound. We report point-by-point laser Doppler vibrometry on the reeds of six handmade hulusi, two each in the keys of F, B$\flat$ and C, measured at 29 points on every reed or tongue over nine fingerings and two supply pressures. Steady-state spectra carry two components: a tube-dominant frequency $f_\mathrm{tube}$, locked to the air-column resonance and carrying a complete harmonic series, and a reed-dominant frequency $f_\mathrm{reed}$, which is not an integer multiple of it. Their difference $Δ= f_\mathrm{tube} - f_\mathrm{reed}$ runs from 38 to 523~Hz across the dataset, from about three semitones to more than an octave. The reed-dominant frequency rises with the pressure at the reed, by $28.0 \pm 10.3$ Hz/kPa once $f_\mathrm{tube}$ is controlled for. At low pressure supply the oscillation loses its lock to the air column, falls silent for about 100~ms, and returns at the reed frequency within 0.1 Hz. The spatial patterns are forced oscillation shapes of one limit cycle at its fundamental and harmonics rather than eigenmodes: the measured frequencies stand in strict 1:2:3 ratios, far from the bending ratios of a cantilever. The reed-dominant pattern is pure bending and holds across fingerings and supply pressures, whereas the tube-dominant pattern breaks up near the oscillation threshold.

items.headline: Evolutionary dynamics of collective-risk social dilemma game with risk uncertainty and adaptive strategy
items.summary: The collective-risk dilemma game constitutes the leading metaphor for studying the evolution of cooperation in populations of selfish individuals. Although most theoretical studies often consider the risk level as a fixed parameter, this may not fully reflect the uncertain nature of risk detected in real-world scenarios. Motivated by the observation that individuals can infer their game environment and accordingly adjust their actual behavior, here we investigate this game with uncertain risk.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In particular, we introduce a type of adaptive agents who incur an observation cost to infer the risk level during game interactions, and subsequently decide whether to cooperate or defect based on their tolerance thresholds. We first calculate the fixation probabilities of three different strategies in a mutation-free regime. Our results show that adaptive agents are favored by natural selection at low observation costs and moderate tolerance thresholds. Moreover, the fixation of adaptive agents results in higher levels of cooperation when both parameters are relatively low. We then consider behavioral mutation and systematically explore how average cooperation level and group achievement vary with observation costs, tolerance thresholds, and mutation rates. Importantly, the main results remain intact when the mutation is considered. Furthermore, when the tolerance threshold is small, the presence of adaptive agents results in a higher cooperation level and group achievement compared to the traditional setup when only unconditional cooperators and defectors are present. This advantage, however, gradually erodes with an increasing tolerance threshold and these two quantities fall below the levels observed in the classic two-strategy case.

items.headline: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
items.summary: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities.

detail.method_architecture: Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. detail.findings_tradeoffs: The algorithm extends to EF$k$X, achieving a $(2+1/k+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every integer $k\geq1$. items.headline: Current frontiers in mobility and well-being
items.summary: Human mobility has a profound impact on social structure and collective behavior, which allows individuals to reshape group structures in response to strategy information, acting as a double-edged sword for cooperative behavior. It can both disrupt existing cooperative communities and enable individuals to escape adverse environments and seek high-quality interaction partners. This paper surveys current research progress on the impact of mobility on cooperation within the framework of evolutionary game theory, focusing on specific mechanisms of passive escape, dynamic self-organization driven by active choice, and the core trade-off between migration costs and speed.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Mobility, an individual's spatial response to local strategic information that turns location into strategic advantage, influences cooperative evolution by altering interactive information and environmental feedback, consequently affecting sustainable social well-being, such as collective benefits. Under specific conditions, this self-interested behavior at the individual level can foster macrosocial harmony, embodying the unity of individual rationality and collective cooperation. Furthermore, we also discusses inter-layer migration and information routing mechanisms in multilayer networks and extends the perspective to human-machine hybrid systems where mobile agents with information regulation capabilities can serve as information supernodes. Our paper aims to provide a unified framework for understanding mobility as a combined physical and informational driving force in the evolution of cooperation.
